blocks.prompt: The City Built by Tiny Animals
blocks.text: A coral reef looks like a garden of stone. But every branch is built by animals. They are called polyps. A polyp is soft, like a tiny finger with arms on top. Each polyp builds a hard cup around itself. The cup is its house. When a polyp dies, its cup stays behind. A new polyp grows on top. Cup on top of cup, for thousands of years. That is how a reef gets big. Fish come to live in it. Crabs hide in the holes. The reef is a busy town under the water.

blocks.prompt: The Animals That Build Cities
blocks.text:
If you touch a coral reef, it feels like stone. It is stone, in a way. But something soft and alive made every bit of it.

A coral polyp is a small animal. It is not much bigger than a pencil eraser. It has a soft body, a mouth on top, and a ring of little arms called tentacles. Polyps are cousins of jellyfish, and like jellyfish, their arms can sting.

Here is the clever part. A polyp pulls minerals out of the sea water and turns them into a hard stone cup. It sits in the cup like a hermit crab in a shell. Thousands of polyps sit side by side, each in its own cup, all joined together. When a polyp dies, its cup stays. A young polyp settles on top and builds a new one.

Cup on cup on cup, for thousands of years. That is a reef. Some reefs took eight thousand years to grow as tall as they are now. They grow slower than your fingernails.

blocks.prompt: The Partner Living in the Wall
blocks.text:
Reach out and touch a reef and you will feel stone, but a reef is not a rock formation. It is a city, and the builders are still living in it.

Each builder is a coral polyp: a soft animal roughly the size of a pencil eraser, with a mouth ringed by stinging tentacles. Polyps belong to the same family as jellyfish and sea anemones. A polyp draws calcium and carbonate out of sea water and cements them into a hard limestone cup, then lives inside it. Millions of polyps, each in its own cup, all fused together, make the branches and boulders you see.

But polyps have a secret partner. Inside the flesh of every reef-building polyp live crowds of microscopic algae called zooxanthellae. The algae catch sunlight and make sugar, the way a leaf does. They hand most of that sugar to the polyp, and in return the polyp gives them a safe place to live and the waste chemicals they need. Up to nine tenths of a coral's food arrives this way. The algae also give coral much of its color.

This partnership explains something strange. Coral reefs only grow in clear, shallow, sunlit water, even though the polyp itself hunts at night and does not need the sun. The reef needs sunlight because its lodgers do.

It also explains a warning sign. When the sea gets too warm, the algae start producing chemicals that harm the polyp, and the polyp throws them out. The coral turns bone white. That is called bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead yet. It is starving, and waiting for its partners to come back.

answers: the algae give sugar made from sunlight; the polyp gives shelter and the waste chemicals they need
(the stone is made by animals that are still alive on its surface, unlike a rock)

(inference: the polyps are alive but have lost the partners that feed them, so they can recover if the algae return)

blocks.prompt: A City Under the Water
blocks.text:
A coral reef looks like scenery. It is closer to a city, and like any city it was built, it is inhabited, and it can fall.

The builders are coral polyps, soft animals no larger than a pencil eraser, each one a relative of the jellyfish. A polyp extracts calcium and carbonate from sea water and cements them into a cup of limestone, then settles inside. Its neighbors do the same, millions of them, all connected. When a polyp dies its cup remains, and a new polyp settles on the roof of the old one. A reef is therefore a stack of skeletons with a thin skin of living animals stretched over the top. The Great Barrier Reef, off the coast of Queensland in Australia, is more than fourteen hundred miles of this. It is the largest structure on Earth made by living things, and you can see it from orbit.

No polyp could afford this on its own. Inside the tissue of every reef-building coral live millions of single-celled algae called zooxanthellae. They photosynthesize, and they pass as much as ninety percent of the sugar they make to their host. In exchange they get shelter and chemicals. This trade is the engine of the whole reef, and it is why reefs need clear, shallow, sunlit water.

The return on that engine is absurd. Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor and shelter about a quarter of all marine species. They also absorb wave energy before it reaches the shore, which protects coastlines and the people on them.

The trade has one weakness. Warm the water by a couple of degrees for a few weeks and the algae turn harmful, the polyps expel them, and the coral goes white. Bleaching is not death. It is eviction, and a bleached coral starves unless conditions cool and its partners return. The animal that built a structure visible from space cannot survive a warm summer alone.

blocks.prompt: The City That Builds Itself, and the Bargain That Holds It Up
blocks.text:
A coral reef is the only city on Earth whose buildings are also its citizens.

Start with the builder. A coral polyp is a soft-bodied animal about the size of a pencil eraser, a mouth encircled by stinging tentacles, and a close relative of the jellyfish and the sea anemone. What separates it from those cousins is a chemical habit. The polyp pulls dissolved calcium and carbonate out of sea water and lays them down beneath itself as crystalline limestone, building a cup, and then lives in the cup it has made. Its neighbors do the same. Millions of polyps, tissue-linked and cup-joined, form a single sheet of living animal spread across a mass of stone that earlier polyps left behind. When a polyp dies, its cup remains and becomes foundation. Larvae settle on the roof of the dead and start again. A reef, then, is a stack of skeletons with a living skin. The Great Barrier Reef is fourteen hundred miles of exactly this, the largest structure any living thing has ever built, and its present form has been accumulating for roughly eight thousand years.

Now the bargain. No polyp could pay for that construction by hunting alone. Inside the tissue of every reef-building coral live millions of single-celled algae called zooxanthellae. The algae photosynthesize in the shallow sunlight and deliver as much as ninety percent of the sugar they produce to their host, while the polyp supplies shelter, carbon dioxide, and the nitrogen waste the algae need. It is one of the most productive partnerships in nature, and it explains a puzzle. Tropical sea water is famously poor in nutrients, close to a desert. Reefs flourish there anyway, because a reef does not eat the ocean. It farms the sun.

The numbers this bargain generates are hard to believe. Coral reefs occupy less than one percent of the ocean floor and shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species. They break wave energy before it lands, protecting coastlines and the millions of people who live along them. They feed fisheries that feed nations. All of it rests on a trade between an animal you can barely see and a plant-like cell living inside its skin.

And that is the vulnerability. The partnership is calibrated finely. Push sea temperature about two degrees above the usual summer maximum for a few weeks and the algae's photosynthesis misfires, producing compounds that damage the polyp's tissue. The polyp expels its tenants. The coral, now transparent over white limestone, appears to have been bleached. It has not died. It has evicted its own food supply, and it will starve within weeks unless the water cools and the algae return. Mass bleaching events, once rare, have struck the Great Barrier Reef repeatedly since 1998, and the gaps between them have been shrinking faster than a reef can rebuild.

There is a temptation to call this fragile. It is not quite the right word. These animals have been laying limestone since long before the first flowers existed. What is fragile is the specific bargain, and the narrow band of temperature in which the bargain pays. The reef is not delicate. The terms are.
